Chapter 3: The Many Foundations of Morality—Why People Disagree About Right and Wrong
Have you ever stepped into a heated conversation about politics or religion, and felt like everyone was talking past each other? It’s not just about facts or who’s better at arguing. What’s really going on is that people are coming from completely different moral worlds.
What seems like pure common sense to you might sound shocking—or even offensive—to someone else. And it’s not just because folks are being stubborn or ignoring the obvious. It goes much deeper, right down to how our minds build ideas of right and wrong from a bunch of basic moral building blocks.
Think of these foundations like the flavors of your favorite dish. Each one is distinct, but most of the time, they’re mixed together in unique ways for every person. Some people are really tuned in to issues of care and harm—they feel a powerful drive to protect the vulnerable and prevent suffering wherever they see it. Others are laser-focused on fairness, making sure everyone follows the same rules and gets what they deserve. Then you’ve got loyalty, authority, and sanctity in the mix. These shape how we think about tradition, respect for hierarchy, and what we consider pure or sacred.
Imagine a fierce debate over a new law. One person might zero in on whether it’s going to help or hurt people in need. Someone else is worried about whether it undermines authority or throws society out of balance. And another person might be focused on whether the law violates something they see as deeply sacred. Each of them is drawing from a different foundation, and to each one, their concern feels like the most important thing in the world.
These differences aren’t just random quirks. They come from our evolutionary history, and from the lessons we pick up in our culture. In some places, loyalty and respecting authority are huge—those values help groups stick together when times get tough. In other societies, it’s all about individual rights and personal freedom, which fuels creativity and the courage to challenge the status quo. Over time, these big-picture priorities get woven into everything from laws to everyday habits.
If you look at political arguments, you’ll often see these moral differences at work. People with progressive views usually put care and fairness at the top of the list, fighting to protect individuals and promote equality. Folks with more conservative leanings tend to value loyalty, authority, and sanctity, believing these hold society together and keep us grounded. The tricky part is, both groups genuinely think they’re standing up for what’s right—but they’re often missing each other’s point entirely.
This stuff isn’t just theoretical. You can see it play out in real life. In one neighborhood, parents might push for stricter rules to keep kids safe, putting safety and purity first. Somewhere else, activists might rally for more freedom and fairness, challenging traditions they see as unfair. Both groups care deeply—but they’re motivated by different moral priorities.
The thing is, most of us don’t realize just how many moral foundations there are. We assume everyone sees the world the way we do, and when someone disagrees, we chalk it up to ignorance or bad intentions. That makes it nearly impossible to meet in the middle, since each side feels misunderstood—or even attacked.
So, what’s the big takeaway? Understanding these different moral foundations doesn’t mean you have to let go of your own beliefs. It just gives you a new lens to see where others are coming from, and why some issues really set people off. When you recognize that your opponents are driven by real moral concerns—even if they’re not the same as yours—it becomes a whole lot easier to have respectful, productive conversations.
